title: The Soul and Immortality
lead: What the Bible means by "soul," and whether the human soul lives on after death by its own nature or by God's gift. Hebrew nephesh is often simply "life" or "a living being"; Greek psychē, especially in the Wisdom of Solomon and the New Testament, can mean the inner self that survives death. Churches agree that eternal life comes from God, but differ on whether the soul is immortal in itself.

sections.b: In Genesis the LORD God shaped the man from dust and breathed into him, "and the man became a living being" (Genesis 2:7): the Hebrew is nephesh chayyah. The man does not receive a soul; he becomes one. Nephesh often means a person's life (Genesis 35:18, where Rachel's life goes out of her) or the person himself: "The person who sins, that very person will die" (Ezekiel 18:4). Many scholars therefore say the Hebrew Bible sees a human being as a unity of body and breath, not a soul housed in a body.

The Greek Bible translated nephesh as psychē, a word that in Greek philosophy meant the inner self, which Plato held to be immortal by nature. The Wisdom of Solomon, written in Greek by a Jew of Alexandria, uses the word in that fuller sense: "the souls of the righteous are in God's hand" (Wisdom 3:1), and a perishable body weighs down the soul (Wisdom 9:15). Yet the book ties immortality to God and to righteousness rather than to the soul's nature (Wisdom 1:15; Wisdom 2:23). Jesus says, "do not fear the people who kill the body but have no power to kill the soul" (Matthew 10:28), and Revelation sees "the souls of those who had been slaughtered" under the altar (Revelation 6:9).
sections.refs: Wisdom 3:1-9; Wisdom 9:15; Wisdom 1:15; Wisdom 2:23; Matthew 10:28; Revelation 6:9-11; Luke 12:20

sections.b: The New Testament says that God "alone has life that cannot die" (1 Timothy 6:16) and that Christ "has brought life and immortality out into the light" (2 Timothy 1:10). Immortality is something to seek (Romans 2:7) and something the dying body "has to put on" at the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:53). The Bible's central hope is the resurrection of the body, not the survival of the soul alone. Christians have read these texts in two ways: that the soul is immortal by nature, created so by God, and will be joined again to the body; or that no part of a human is immortal until God gives life to the saved. The second view, conditional immortality, is taught by Seventh-day Adventists and some other Protestants; Jehovah's Witnesses teach that the soul is the whole person and dies.

Three questions are linked but separate. (1) Is the soul immortal by nature or by God's gift? See the card at Wisdom 3. (2) Are the dead conscious between death and the resurrection? See the topic on the state between death and resurrection and the cards at 2 Corinthians 5 and Revelation 6. (3) Did souls exist before their bodies? The Wisdom of Solomon raises it at 8:19-20, where its card is.
